title: The Phulkian states
hook: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, often counted apart from the twelve

segments.voice: Yesterday, shaheed, the martyr, and a band that kept the martyrs' memory; your line was the martyrs' band. Today, a family of chiefs who stood a little to one side.

A hungry boy is brought before Guru Har Rai. Sikh tradition tells it simply: an uncle brings two small brothers to the Guru, and one of them pats his own empty stomach. The Guru looks at the child and blesses him: his house will grow, and it will feed many. The boy's name was Phul. Generations later, the families who traced their line to him ruled three states south of the Sutlej: Patiala, Nabha and Jind.
screen: `A HUNGRY BOY BEFORE GURU HAR RAI.` → `A BLESSING ON HIS HOUSE.` → `PATIALA, NABHA AND JIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. Some lists of the twelve misls include the Phulkian states; others set them apart. Both habits have reasons. One is the river. The Phulkian chiefs held the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej: different neighbors, different dangers, different deals. Another is how they ruled. A misl was a band of equals around a chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. The Phulkian houses grew more like ruling families, leadership passing down a line, the chief becoming a raja. Patiala's founder, Ala Singh, is remembered for building a state, and for making terms with the powers around him at times when other bands were fighting them. Sikh histories judge those terms in more than one way: some call them shrewd survival, some a step away from the Dal Khalsa. So why are they here at all? Because the story starts with the Guru's blessing. The Phulkian families traced their rise to that hungry boy, and they built and supported gurdwaras across their lands. They stood apart in politics and stayed inside the same faith, the same scripture, the same Guru's house. A family can live in a different town and still sit at the same table on the big days.
screen: `SOME LISTS COUNT THEM, SOME DON'T.` · `SOUTH OF THE SUTLEJ, IN MALWA.` · `RULING FAMILIES, NOT BANDS OF EQUALS.` · `ONE GURU'S HOUSE STILL.` · then, large: `APART, YET RELATED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a group you belong to, a family, a team, a congregation, and find the person who stands a little to the side of it: the cousin who moved away, the coworker who eats lunch alone. Don't fix anything; just hold them in mind and notice what still connects them to the rest. Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.
Phul, the boy Guru Har Rai blessed, whose line the Phulkian states, Patiala, Nabha and Jind, traced their rule to. Counted with the misls by some, set apart by others. Today's word.
Your line: apart, yet related. Politics apart, faith shared. That's day eight hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 899 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWICE A YEAR AT AMRITSAR.`

howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the story of Phul and Guru Har Rai's blessing, and gurdwaras in the former Phulkian lands, such as those in Patiala, are part of Sikh life in the Malwa region today.

chat.says: Are the Phulkian states one of the twelve misls or not?
options: Some lists count them, others set them apart: ruling families south of the Sutlej, one faith.
Never. They left the Sikh faith after making terms with the powers around them.
Always. Every list puts them among the twelve, as bands of equals like the rest.
chat.meaning: Some lists include them and others set them apart; they ruled as families but stayed in the same faith.

notes: The Phul story: tellings differ on who brought the boys (Phul and his brother Sandali) and the exact words of the blessing; framed as 'tradition tells it' with variants. Confirm.
The meaning of the name Phul (flower) was cut under the claims rule.
The index says the Phulkian states are 'often counted apart from the twelve'; many standard lists include Phulkian as one of the twelve misls. The script says both habits exist. Confirm.

Ala Singh 'making terms with the powers around him' (including Ahmad Shah Abdali) and Sikh histories judging this 'in more than one way': this is sensitive; a Keeper should confirm the framing is fair to Patiala and to its critics.
'Built and supported gurdwaras across their lands': general; confirm.

Editor: removed the claim that all the other misls held land north of the Sutlej (day 898's Shaheedan were centered at Damdama Sahib, in Malwa); myth item changed to match; softened Ala Singh's terms to 'at times when other bands were fighting them'.

Audit: hook's 'a mother, or an uncle in some tellings' cut to 'an uncle' (the usual tellings name the boys' uncle, Kala; the mother variant could not be supported). Fork no longer casts the listener as Guru Har Rai, since many Sikhs avoid depicting or role-playing the Gurus; the listener is now the uncle. Keeper: confirm.
